cells.tense: You are here with the pen, weighing what a finished piece of work actually produced.
cells.ask: Pick one thing you carried through, say what it really produced, and name what you owe and what's owed to you.
cells.core:
You can tell what's fair without running every number twice. Something you carried through has finished growing, and you're able to look at it as it is — not as you hoped it would be, not as someone else described it. That read arrives cleanly, and you let it move through you instead of standing over it. The exchange settles with a light hand, the way fairness works when it's already working.

What this looks like here is standing in the middle of what you made, with just enough light to see the next step. You don't have to know how the whole thing turns out. You just gather what's ready. Counting what came in, saying what's owed both ways, keeps fairness from becoming a calculation you're trying to win. That's what's available right now, and it doesn't need to be forced.
cells.sheetLine: You can see what your work produced without turning it into a score.
cells.verb: Gathering what transformation grew and evaluating its yield
cells.place: Navigating ambiguity with enough light for the next step

cells.tense: You are reaching for a yield that hasn't come in, pressing the outcome before its time.
cells.ask: Leave one thing you're pushing toward unforced for a full day, and notice what shifts without your hand on it.
cells.core:
The work you're waiting on is still coming in, and you're already sizing it up. You're comparing what it should produce to what's on the table now, and the gap is filling with pressure. The waiting that got something here is being spent trying to skip the wait. A conversation turns into a report on progress. A quiet hour turns into proof that something's wrong.

There's a way of sitting with what you know that doesn't need the result in hand, and this is the moment for it. Not pushing doesn't mean doing nothing. It means letting one thing stay unforced while it comes in. The harvest doesn't turn faster because you're watching it, and you're the one who has to be here when it turns. You can take your hand off the scale for a day.

cells.tense: You are standing in front of something already grown, and you haven't reached for it yet.
cells.ask: Take one step you've been waiting to feel ready for, and let the next step show itself after you move.
cells.core:
Something has already changed and produced what it was going to produce, and the step of picking it up hasn't started. You've been keeping your footing in one spot while the harvest sits there. The work that got it to here is done. What isn't happening is the picking up. Feeling your way through isn't the trouble.

The trouble is you've stopped moving. Direction comes from being engaged with what's in front of you, and you've been reading from a place you already left. Take one step without a clear view of the whole path. Not because the path will open for you, but because that's how paths show themselves — one part at a time, after you've walked. The next part is not visible from where you're standing now.

cells.tense: You are already shaping how results get counted here while calling it just the way things work.
cells.ask: Describe one structure you set up — a rule, an agreement, a way things are counted — and claim it out loud as yours.
cells.core:
You've already built the arrangement that holds these results. How work gets counted, how people know what's fair, who owes what to whom — that didn't fall out of the sky. You decided. You talk about it like it's simply the way things are, like the field grew itself and you happen to be standing in it. Meanwhile the people near you are reading the field by your signs.

That arrangement is real, and it's doing what you designed it to do. The unclaimed part is the making of it. Saying it out loud doesn't make you proud. It puts the pen back where it belongs. That's the whole step: naming one thing you set up and taking it back.
